Chapter One: Growing Up in a Changing World—Early Life and the Seeds of Compassion.
Before anyone ever heard her name, before her words would echo through history, there was just a young girl growing up in a world that seemed to shift and tremble beneath her feet.
Imagine being a child, living in the shadow of a world war. In a small Austrian town, she learned early what hunger felt like, what it meant to worry about the future. But she also discovered something powerful—the way families pull together when everything else feels uncertain.
When she was still young, her parents made a heartbreaking decision. Out of love and necessity, they sent her to live with a Dutch family in Amsterdam. The separation was tough—no one ever really gets used to saying goodbye to home—but this new chapter taught her about kindness in unexpected places.
The Dutch family welcomed her with open arms. She learned to speak a new language, to adjust to unfamiliar traditions, and to find comfort in the steady rhythm of daily life. With every friendly gesture, she realized that sometimes, the biggest acts of compassion come from people who don’t have to help at all.
As the years went by, the world changed yet again. The rise of the Nazi regime in Germany sent shockwaves across Europe, and Amsterdam—once a place of safety—began to feel uneasy. She found work in an office, where she crossed paths with people from all walks of life. There, she met a gentle, thoughtful man who would become her husband. Together, they carved out a modest life, savoring small joys and the warmth of close friendships.
But the city itself was changing. The Jewish community, once lively and woven into the city’s fabric, now faced new laws and growing suspicion. Many of her friends and coworkers were Jewish, and she watched, helpless, as their freedoms were slowly chipped away. The world she knew was slipping away, replaced by a climate of fear and mistrust.
Through it all, the lessons from her childhood stuck with her—resilience, adaptability, and the quiet power of kindness. She noticed how easy it was for people to look the other way, to hope someone else would step in. But she also saw the quiet bravery of those who couldn’t ignore another’s suffering, the ones who reached out, even when it was risky or inconvenient.
The city’s streets became tense, soldiers patrolled the sidewalks, and whispers about disappearances drifted from door to door. Yet, even in these uncertain times, she clung to one belief: ordinary people can make a difference. The world might be changing, but the need for compassion? That never fades.
